vignette:
Tavita is a 45-year-old Samoan American man who had spent most of his adult life in restaurant kitchens, where his sense of himself was bound up with speed, endurance, and command. Before the assault, he had been proud of being the chef who could carry a service through chaos, barking orders over the stove line and plating with steady hands even when tickets stacked up. He was divorced, living alone, and had built much of his identity around work. The rape happened late one night after a shift, when he stayed behind with someone he knew through the restaurant scene. In telling it now, he does not struggle to begin; he can say plainly what was done to him and where it happened. But as he gets further into the account, the sequence loosens. He jumps from the locked back room to the smell of bleach on the prep counter, then to the feeling of being pinned, then back again, and often cuts himself off before the memory fully unfolds, as if he cannot bear to let it run to the end.

In the weeks afterward, what took hold most strongly was not only fear but a collapse in how he saw himself. Tavita had come to believe that something essential in him had been ruined. He said, with flat certainty, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. In the kitchen, where he once moved decisively, he now felt exposed in his own body, as if his authority had been stripped away. He also carried a persistent sense of contamination. The smells and textures that used to belong to his craft-raw meat, damp towels, the heat and sweat of service-began to feel fouled. Sometimes after work he showered repeatedly, scrubbing at his skin with enough force to leave it red, not because he thought it would change anything, but because he could not shake the feeling of being dirty. Over time, these beliefs hardened into a broader conviction that the assault had destroyed his life.

Those conclusions shape the way he remembers what happened. When Tavita starts to talk about the assault, he can do so easily in one sense, almost too easily at first, in a clipped factual way that sounds practiced. But once he approaches the parts that matter most to him-the moments that confirm, in his mind, that he was overpowered, defiled, and no longer the man he had been-his mind seems to fragment around them. He loses the order of events and says he cannot get the pieces to line up correctly. He will stop mid-sentence, look away, and push the memory aside before it is complete. What frightens him is not simply recalling it; it is what a full recollection seems to prove. In his mind, if he lets himself know the whole thing, it will only confirm that his life is over and that he is permanently contaminated. The more he sees himself through that lens, the harder it becomes for him to hold the memory together from beginning to end.

This has altered his life in concrete ways. As a chef, he still works around the very conditions that now unsettle him: cramped spaces, closing shifts, stainless-steel prep areas after the rush has ended. At the restaurant, being alone in the walk-in or asked to finish inventory in the back can be enough to make him feel sick and abruptly leave the area. His coworkers have noticed that he avoids staying late and gives away tasks he once insisted on doing himself. He interprets these changes as further proof that he is no longer capable, and that belief deepens his shame. The kitchen, once the place where he felt most like himself, has become the daily setting in which he confronts what he thinks has been taken from him.

By the time he came for help, Tavita had been living for months in a narrow cycle of work, isolation, and self-disgust. He could speak about the rape, but not in a way that felt resolved or complete; the story remained broken apart, interrupted at the points where his own meanings about it became unbearable. He sought treatment after realizing he was close to quitting the only work he had ever loved. What he fears most is that the assault has permanently destroyed the man he was and left him unfit for the life he built. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that there might still be some way to remember what happened without it serving as final proof that he is ruined.
